items.explanation: McCarthy's censure in 1954 damaged one man, not the machinery of anti-communism. The House Un-American Activities Committee kept operating into the 1970s, loyalty programs persisted, and anti-communist politics continued -- so 1954 was not an endpoint. The censure punished McCarthy's conduct rather than rejecting anti-communism, one court narrowing did not end the legal campaign, and softer rhetoric did not mean vanished politics.
items.fact_source: Senate censure of McCarthy, December 1954; HUAC operated 1938-1975; Yates v. United States (1957) narrowed Smith Act prosecutions without ending loyalty programs; McCarran Internal Security Act (1950) remained law.

option_explanations.A: Right. HUAC kept investigating alleged subversives for two more decades, which directly contradicts the claim that anti-communism effectively ended in 1954.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Senate censured McCarthy's conduct, not anti-communism itself; one vote against one man does not show officials rejected the broader cause.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Yates narrowed how the Smith Act could be used in prosecutions, but it did not end federal or state loyalty programs.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. That later presidents used softer language does not prove anti-communism vanished; rhetoric is not the same as policy.

options: (A) The House Un-American Activities Committee continued to investigate alleged subversives into the 1970s
(B) The Senate censured McCarthy by a large bipartisan vote, which shows elected officials had turned against anti-communism itself
(C) The Supreme Court limited Smith Act prosecutions in Yates v. United States (1957), which proves the legal campaign against communism had ended
(D) Later presidents spoke about freedom more than about hunting communists, which proves anti-communism had vanished from American politics
items.stem: A student argues that anti-communist sentiment in the United States effectively ended in 1954, when the Senate censured Joseph McCarthy. Which piece of evidence would most directly challenge this claim?

items.explanation: The domino theory predicted that one communist victory would topple neighboring states. After the American withdrawal, communist governments did take power in South Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia in 1975 -- but Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, and the Philippines did not follow. The student's claim ignores the first half of that record, so it needs qualification rather than acceptance or rejection; and knowing the outcome now does not make the theory 'obviously wrong' to those deciding in the 1960s.
items.fact_source: Fall of Saigon, Pathet Lao takeover of Laos, and Khmer Rouge takeover of Cambodia, all 1975; Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, and the Philippines did not become communist.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Communist governments did take power in South Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia in 1975 -- the claim's key fact is mistaken.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Where the domino theory came from does not determine whether it was right; dismissing an idea because of its proponents' motives avoids evaluating the claim.
option_explanations.C: Right. The argument overstates its case: Laos and Cambodia did fall to communist governments in 1975, though the wider cascade the theory predicted never happened.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Judging 1960s decisions with 1975 knowledge is hindsight -- and it still ignores that Laos and Cambodia did come under communist rule.

options: (A) The argument is accurate: after 1975, no Southeast Asian nation came under communist rule
(B) The argument is accurate because American leaders invented the domino theory to justify the war, so the war's outcome discredits the theory itself
(C) The argument needs qualification: Laos and Cambodia did come under communist rule in 1975, though Thailand, Indonesia, and others did not follow.
(D) The argument is flawed because Thailand, Indonesia, and Malaysia never fell, which proves the domino theory was obviously wrong from the start and policymakers should have known it
items.stem: A student argues: 'The Vietnam War disproved the domino theory. Once American forces left, no other Southeast Asian country became communist.' Which statement best evaluates this argument?

items.explanation: King's audience was the white moderates who counseled 'wait,' and his purpose was to make delay morally indefensible while appealing to national opinion — not to negotiate ordinances with the segregationist city government. The letter came four months before the March on Washington, was not addressed to activists, and defended breaking unjust laws, not all laws.
items.fact_source: 'Letter from Birmingham Jail,' April 16, 1963, addressed to eight Alabama clergymen who had called the demonstrations 'unwise and untimely'; March on Washington, August 28, 1963.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The named audience — clergymen who called the protests 'unwise and untimely' — shows King was pressuring moderates, not petitioning segregationist officials.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The March on Washington took place in August 1963, four months after the April letter; the letter cannot have responded to it.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The letter's stated audience is the eight clergymen, not movement activists; its purpose was outward persuasion, not internal explanation.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. King explicitly distinguished just from unjust laws and accepted the penalty for breaking the latter; he did not reject all law.

options: (A) The letter targets moderate clergymen who urged patience, not segregationist officials.
(B) The letter was written in response to criticism King received after the March on Washington.
(C) King wrote the letter to explain nonviolent philosophy to fellow civil rights activists.
(D) The letter's distinction between just and unjust laws shows King rejected the authority of all laws.
items.stem: A student claims the letter was written mainly to persuade Birmingham's segregationist officials to repeal the city's segregation ordinances. Which fact about the letter's situation best challenges that claim?

stimulus.text: [Paraphrased from Martin Luther King Jr., 'Letter from Birmingham Jail,' April 1963:] Writing from jail, King answers eight white Alabama clergymen who called the Birmingham demonstrations 'unwise and untimely.' He argues that 'justice too long delayed is justice denied' and that nonviolent direct action creates the crisis and tension a community needs before it will negotiate.

items.explanation: Levitt's mass-produced suburbs, bought with federally insured mortgages, show the two halves of the claim working together: federal policy supplied the financing, private developers supplied the houses. (A) gives highways the whole job -- they helped, but they did not finance or build the homes. (B) imagines an equal-opportunity suburbia that redlining and restrictive practices contradict. (C) scrambles the timeline: Levittown was selling houses years before the 1956 highway act.
items.fact_source: FHA/VA mortgage insurance under the National Housing Act and the Servicemen's Readjustment Act (GI Bill, 1944); Levitt & Sons developments (Levittown, NY, 1947-51, predating the 1956 highway act); Interstate Highway Act of 1956; redlining and racially restrictive covenants excluded Black buyers from many suburbs.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Highways made commuting practical, but they neither financed the mortgages nor built the houses -- one cause cannot explain a two-part claim.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Federal policy did not help everyone equally: redlining and restrictive covenants shut Black buyers out of many of the very suburbs the policy helped build.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The timeline is backwards -- Levittown was selling houses in the late 1940s, years before the 1956 highway act.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Federally insured mortgages flowing into privately built, mass-produced developments is direct evidence of the policy-plus-developer combination the historian describes.

options: (A) The Interstate Highway Act of 1956 caused suburbanization by itself, since new highways alone were enough to create the suburbs.
(B) Federal housing policy helped all Americans equally, so suburban growth shows the postwar economy worked the same for every group.
(C) Real suburban growth began only after the Interstate Highway Act of 1956, so earlier developments like Levittown were not truly part of the suburban boom.
(D) Developers like Levitt built whole suburbs for buyers using FHA- and VA-insured mortgages.
items.stem: A historian argues that 1950s suburban growth is best explained by federal housing policy and private developers working together to meet a severe housing shortage. Which finding would most directly support this claim?

items.explanation: An eight-year gap filled with oil spills, a burning river, and a mass mobilization shows the EPA resulted from many pressures, not one book. Silent Spring mattered, but 'leading directly' skips the intervening events that turned concern into a political force. The other options misdate events, overread executive action, or confuse 1960s environmentalism with the earlier conservation movement.
items.fact_source: Rachel Carson, Silent Spring (1962); Carson testified before a Senate subcommittee in 1963 and died in 1964; Santa Barbara oil spill, January 1969; Cuyahoga River fire, June 1969; first Earth Day, April 22, 1970; EPA established December 1970 via Reorganization Plan No. 3.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Carson did testify in 1963, but she died in 1964; linking her testimony directly to a 1970 law collapses seven years of intervening history into a single cause.
option_explanations.B: Correct. These events between 1962 and 1970 built the broad public pressure that made the EPA politically possible, so the book alone cannot explain its creation.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The EPA was indeed created by executive reorganization, but Nixon acted amid massive public pressure — Earth Day drew millions in April 1970 — so the method of creation does not erase the public's role.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Pollution of air and water was central to 1960s environmentalism; wilderness preservation was the focus of the earlier conservation movement, not the 1960s.

options: (A) Carson testified before Congress in 1963, which led directly to the Clean Air Act of 1970.
(B) The Santa Barbara oil spill, the Cuyahoga fire, and the first Earth Day fell between the book and the EPA.
(C) Nixon created the EPA by executive order, which proves public pressure played no part in its establishment.
(D) Environmental activism in the 1960s was concerned only with preserving wilderness, not with pollution.
items.stem: A textbook states: 'Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962) awakened the public to pesticide dangers, leading directly to the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency in 1970.' Which observation best qualifies this account?

items.explanation: Smith criticized McCarthy's methods, not the anticommunist cause itself, and almost no Senate Republicans joined her. The speech therefore shows rare dissent inside an anticommunist consensus, not a Republican turn against anticommunism. Using it as evidence of widespread opposition overreads both the author's position and her isolation.
items.fact_source: Margaret Chase Smith, 'Declaration of Conscience,' Congressional Record, June 1, 1950; six other Republican senators signed the declaration (Senate Historical Office). McCarthy was censured December 1954 and died in office May 1957; Army-McCarthy hearings were televised April-June 1954.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Smith supported investigating genuine security threats and objected only to smear tactics, and just six fellow Republicans signed her declaration — so the speech cannot show broad Republican rejection of anticommunism.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The Army-McCarthy hearings were televised in 1954, four years after this speech; the speech cannot have been a reaction to them.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. One senator's appeal does not establish what most Americans valued, and projecting modern civil-liberties priorities onto 1950 ignores how widely anticommunism was supported at the time.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. McCarthy kept his Senate seat until his death in 1957; he was censured by the Senate in 1954, not removed, and the speech did not end the Red Scare.

options: (A) Smith remained a committed anticommunist, and only a handful of Republican senators endorsed her statement.
(B) The speech was delivered in reaction to the televised Army-McCarthy hearings.
(C) Smith's appeal to conscience shows that most Americans in 1950 valued civil liberties above national security.
(D) The speech caused McCarthy to lose his Senate seat, ending the Red Scare.
items.stem: A historian writing about domestic anticommunism in the early Cold War cites this speech as evidence that many Republicans had turned against anticommunism by 1950. Which consideration most limits this use of the source?

stimulus.text: [Paraphrased from Margaret Chase Smith (R-ME), 'Declaration of Conscience,' Senate speech, June 1, 1950:] 'I do not want to see the Republican Party ride to political victory on the four horsemen of calumny — fear, ignorance, bigotry, and smear. I am not proud of the way we have used the issue of communism for partisan advantage.'

items.explanation: If opposition was already climbing through 1967, Tet coverage cannot be the primary cause of the collapse; at most it sped up a trend already underway. (A) shrinks a complex shift to a single broadcast and a single conversation. (B) treats television as a transparent window, ignoring that what viewers saw depended on what cameras showed and how it was framed. (D) gets the battle backwards -- Tet was a tactical defeat for the communists -- and confuses battlefield results with what moves public opinion.
items.fact_source: Gallup 'mistake' polling trend, 1965-1968; Walter Cronkite, 'Report from Vietnam,' CBS, February 27, 1968; the 'Cronkite lost the war' account is an oversimplification of a complex shift; Tet (January 1968) was a tactical defeat for the Viet Cong and North Vietnam but a political shock in the U.S.; U.S. Census data on television household penetration (about 90% by the mid-1960s).

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The famous Cronkite-Johnson story shrinks a years-long shift in public opinion to one broadcast and one conversation -- a single anecdote cannot carry the whole causal claim.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Cameras do not simply show reality; what viewers saw depended on what was filmed, selected, and framed. Treating television as a neutral window misses how coverage shapes what it shows.
option_explanations.C: Correct. A steady pre-Tet rise in opposition shows the collapse was underway before the offensive, so television coverage of Tet cannot be its primary cause.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Tet was a tactical defeat for the communists, not for the Americans -- and battlefield results are not the same as public opinion, which is what the historian's claim is about.

options: (A) Walter Cronkite personally convinced President Johnson the war was lost, proving that a single television broadcast ended his presidency.
(B) Television cameras in 1968 showed the war exactly as it happened, so viewers who turned against the war were responding to plain facts rather than to how the war was presented to them.
(C) National polls showed opposition to the war rising steadily through 1967, before the Tet Offensive.
(D) The Tet Offensive was a major American military defeat, so the collapse of public support needs no explanation beyond the battlefield loss.
items.stem: A historian argues that television coverage of the Tet Offensive was the primary cause of the collapse of American public support for the Vietnam War. Which evidence would most directly qualify this argument?
